question: How does Schwab utilize its scale to cheaply acquire new clients and how could Edward Jones replicate a similar strategy?

claims.text: Schwab uses its scale to spread operating costs over a large client base and create a cost advantage that enables competitive pricing while profitably serving clients across channels.

Schwab cites its scale and expense discipline, data-led marketing, and cost-to-serve efficiency as keeping it the industry leader in expense on client assets, with marketing driving about 40% of new-to-firm retail clients.
Edward Jones acquires clients through its branch office model of personal relationships and through initiatives targeting High Net Worth, Workplace, and Next Generation investors.
Edward Jones's operating expenses rose 11% to $15,610 million in 2025, driven by compensation and benefits, variable compensation, and communications and data processing expense.

Whether Edward Jones could replicate Schwab's strategy cannot be determined from this evidence, because the sources describe Schwab's scale advantages and Edward Jones's advisor-based model but contain no disclosed comparison of the two firms' acquisition economics.

adjacent.text: Schwab reports GAAP cost per client account of $442 in 2020, and states its cost per client account has decreased more than 25% over the last decade and 20% over the last five years.
adjacent.differs_because: This is cost per client account, not the cost of acquiring each new client; it reflects the cost to serve the existing account base rather than an acquisition cost per new client.

adjacent.text: Schwab reports 2026 year-to-date core net new assets and new brokerage accounts figures in its third-quarter 2026 deck.
